sections.heading: Seeing your greatness and still coming near
sections.text:
All-sufficient King, when I come to you, help me remember who I am speaking to. You reign over everything, forever. You are surrounded by more servants than I can imagine, and nothing in creation is outside your rule.

Let your greatness settle deeply in my mind—not so I run away from you, but so I come to you with awe. Don’t let your majesty make me less confident in your mercy. Let it make me wonder all the more that you would welcome someone like me.
theological_themes: God reigns as the supreme King over all creation.
God’s majesty should produce reverent confidence, not distance, because he graciously welcomes his people.

scripture_references.connection: This passage holds together the greatness of Christ and the believer’s bold approach to God. Because Jesus is the great high priest, God’s holiness does not push his people away but invites them to come for mercy and help.
John’s vision of countless heavenly beings worshiping the Lamb gives biblical shape to the prayer’s sense of God’s overwhelming glory and the vast company that serves and praises him.

sections.heading: Remembering how carefully you have kept me
sections.text:
You have paid attention to me. You have cared for me from the beginning of my life. In every season—strong or weak, steady or confused, full or empty—you have not dropped me.

You have fed me from your own table. You have surrounded me with love like a shelter drawn close around me. Morning after morning, before I had earned anything or even asked well, you were already giving fresh mercy.
theological_themes: God’s providential care extends across the whole of a believer’s life.
Daily mercy is undeserved and personal, not abstract.

scripture_references.connection: The psalmist traces God’s care back to birth, recognizing that dependence on God did not begin with conscious faith but with God’s prior keeping.
In the middle of suffering, this passage confesses that God’s mercies are renewed each morning. It supports the prayer’s gratitude for daily, repeated mercy rather than one-time help.
The image of God preparing a table and surrounding his people with goodness and mercy closely matches the prayer’s picture of being fed and sheltered by divine love.

sections.heading: Looking beyond this life to what you have given in Christ
sections.text:
Please don’t let me live as if your past care is all I have to hope for. You have promised more than survival and comfort now. You have set before me hope beyond the grave, and even now you give foretastes of the life that is coming.

In Christ, you have provided what I cannot create in myself: holiness, wisdom, strength, peace, and joy. Keep teaching me to look for all of it in him, not in my own resources.
theological_themes: Christian hope reaches beyond death because of God’s saving work in Christ.
Christ is the source of the believer’s holiness, wisdom, strength, peace, and joy.
Present gifts of grace are foretastes of the fullness to come.

scripture_references.connection: Peter grounds the believer’s living hope and future inheritance in God’s mercy and Christ’s resurrection, fitting the prayer’s expectation of blessing beyond the grave.
Paul explicitly names Christ as the one who becomes wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption for believers, supporting the prayer’s claim that these deep needs are provided in Christ.
The Spirit is described as the guarantee of the believer’s inheritance, which helps explain the prayer’s language of present foretastes of immortality and future fullness.

sections.heading: Admitting how little I have responded to you
sections.text:
It grieves me to see how dull and unresponsive I have been. You have every right to rule me, and you have shown me love that should have won my whole heart. Still, I have treated your truth lightly. I have not trusted your promises as I should. I have not taken your warnings seriously. I have ignored commands I knew were good.

I have wasted privileges, brushed past correction, and responded slowly to grace. If I were dealt with only according to what I deserve, I would have no defense. Yet here I am, still alive, still being invited to return to you.
theological_themes: Sin includes unbelief, disobedience, ingratitude, and failure to respond to grace.
God’s continued patience toward sinners is undeserved mercy, not something owed.
True confession takes God’s authority, promises, warnings, and commands seriously.

scripture_references.connection: David’s confession recognizes sin as being ultimately against God, which fits the prayer’s grief over failing to honor God’s authority and love.
This warning addresses the danger of drifting from what God has spoken and neglecting salvation, illuminating the prayer’s confession of treating truth, warnings, and grace too lightly.

sections.heading: Asking your patience to bring me all the way home
sections.text:
Father, let your kindness do its proper work in me. Don’t let me use your patience as an excuse to stay the same. Let your goodness break my hardness and lead me to real repentance.

Keep being patient with me in the way that saves—turning me back, holding me fast, and finishing what you have begun in me. I do not want to presume on your mercy. I want to be changed by it.
theological_themes: God’s kindness is meant to lead sinners to repentance, not complacency.
God’s patience serves his saving purposes in his people.
Perseverance in faith depends on God’s continued grace.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that God’s kindness, forbearance, and patience are meant to lead people to repentance, directly grounding the prayer’s final request.
Peter explains God’s patience in relation to repentance and salvation, supporting the prayer’s plea that divine longsuffering would not be wasted but would bring the person safely to God.
Paul’s confidence that God will complete the work he began supports the prayer’s dependence on God to keep, change, and finish his saving work in the believer.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original uses royal and imperial language for God’s rule, including the phrase “universal empire.” I preserved the theology of God’s absolute sovereignty while avoiding modern political overtones of empire.

The phrase “feared thy threats” can sound harsh in contemporary language, but the original is referring to taking God’s warnings and judgments seriously. I rendered it as “taken your warnings seriously” rather than removing the element of holy fear.

The line “thy longsuffering prove my salvation” could be misunderstood as though patience itself saves apart from Christ. I rendered it as God’s patience serving his saving purpose by leading to repentance and perseverance.
significant_interpretive_choices: I interpreted “condescension” as God’s gracious willingness to welcome and draw near to lowly sinners, not as patronizing behavior, since that is the older theological sense of the word.
I took “improved my advantages” to mean making faithful use of spiritual privileges, opportunities, and warnings, rather than self-improvement in a modern therapeutic sense.
I kept the movement from awe before God’s majesty, to remembrance of lifelong care, to future hope in Christ, to confession, and finally to repentance produced by God’s goodness.
